L26: Exploring the History of the Arctic Council
L27: # Arctic Realities – Global Impacts
L28: ##### 30 years of Arctic Council cooperation.
L29: 
L30: Explore the history of the Arctic Council through the milestones that have defined Arctic cooperation. This timeline highlights the Council's significant achievements and shows how its work has advanced knowledge, strengthened collaboration, and influenced policies in the Arctic and beyond.
L31: Along the way, you'll hear personal reflections from people who have been part of this remarkable journey and discover why the Arctic Council continues to play a vital role in addressing the challenges and opportunities facing the Arctic today.

L131: ### Arctic Environmental Protection Strategy (AEPS) was signed
L132: 
L133: The AEPS was a non-binding agreement between the 8 Arctic States on environmental protection in the Arctic. In the AEPS, three Indigenous Peoples’ organizations- the Sámi Council, Inuit Circumpolar Council and Russian Association of Indigenous Peoples of the North were admitted as Observer organizations. This initial cooperation framework laid the groundwork and directly led to the establishment of the Arctic Council.

L141: 
L142: Created to deliver sound science-based information for use in policy- and decision-making. Its assessment activities are internationally coordinated, subject to rigorous peer-review and make use of the most up-to-date results from both monitoring and research.

L172: ### Indigenous Peoples Secretariat (IPS) Established
L173: 
L174: The IPS was established to support the work of the Indigenous Peoples' organizations in the AEPS. Today, IPS supports all six Indigenous Peoples' organizations with Permanent Participant status in the Arctic Council. The IPS started its operations in December 1994.

L179: ### Signing of the Ottawa Declaration establishes the Arctic Council
L180: 
L181: On September 19, 1996 in Ottawa, Canada, the Arctic Council was established as a high-level intergovernmental forum to enhance cooperation, coordination and interaction among the Arctic States with full consultation and active involvement of Arctic Indigenous Peoples as Permanent Participants, and other Arctic inhabitants on common Arctic issues.

L189: ### New Category Created for Indigenous Peoples' Participation
L190: Recognizing the special relationship of Indigenous Peoples to the Arctic, the category of Permanent Participants was negotiated in the Arctic Council. It gave Indigenous Peoples' organizations full consultation rights in connection with the Council's negotiations and decisions. The category is unique to the Arctic Council and the first time that a category on this level was set up in an international organization.
L191: The first Permanent Participants were the Inuit Circumpolar Council (ICC) – representing People in Alaska, Canada, Greenland (Kalaallit Nunaat), and Chukotka; the Saami Council – representing People in Finland, Russia, Norway and Sweden; and the Russian Association of Indigenous Peoples of the North (RAIPON).

L204: ### Arctic Pollution Issues: A State of the Arctic Environment Report released — the foundation for the Stockholm Convention
L205: 
L206: The first comprehensive circumpolar assessment of Arctic pollution. The report, published by the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme, identified chemicals recommended for international regulation, and has been referred to in literature as the “fundamental building block” of the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, which was being negotiated at the time.

L212: ### The Aleut International Association admitted as a Permanent Participant of the Arctic Council.
L213: 
L214: The Aleut International Association (AIA) represents the Indigenous Peoples of Unangas/Unangan (Aleut) descent in the United States and the Russian Federation. AIA was formed to address environmental and cultural concerns of the extended Unangas/Unangan family whose well-being has been connected to the rich resources of the Bering Sea for millennia.

L218: ### Sustainable Development Working Group (SDWG) was established
L219: 
L220: The goal of the Sustainable Development Working Group of the Arctic Council is to propose and adopt steps to be taken by the Arctic States to advance sustainable development in the Arctic. This includes pursuing opportunities to protect and enhance the environment and the economies, culture and health of Indigenous Peoples and Arctic communities.
L221:

L226: ### First Observers accredited
L227: Observer status in the Arctic Council is open to non-Arctic states, along with inter-governmental, inter-parliamentary, global, regional and non-governmental organizations that the Council determines can contribute to its work. Arctic Council Observers primarily contribute through their engagement at the level of Working Groups.
L228: The first group of Observers accredited were: Germany, The Netherlands, Poland, United Kingdom, Standing Committee of the Parliamentarians of the Arctic Region (SCPAR), United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), International Arctic Science Committee (IASC), International Union for Circumpolar Health (IUCH), Northern Forum (NF), World Wide Fund for Nature, and Arctic Programme (WWF).

L240: ### Arctic Athabaskan Council (AAC) Admitted as a Permanent Participant of the Arctic Council
L241: 
L242: The Arctic Athabaskan Council (AAC) is an International Treaty Organization focused on advancing the interests of Athabaskan Peoples in Alaska and Canada within the eight-nation Arctic Council and other international fora. At its founding, AAC represented approximately 32,000 Indigenous Peoples of Athabaskan descent across Alaska, Yukon, and the Northwest Territories.

L286: ### Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) signed
L287: 
L288: The 2001 Stockholm Convention on POPs was catalyzed by Arctic Council research. POPs are chemicals of global concern. They can travel over long distances, are persistent in the environment, and are able to accumulate in ecosystems, leading to negative effects on human health and the environment.

L310: ### Arctic Climate Impact Assessment (ACIA) released
L311: 
L312: The first comprehensive multi-disciplinary assessment of the impacts of climate change in the Arctic. Nearly 300 scientists, experts, and representatives for Indigenous Peoples’ contributed, combining scientific research with the thoughtful and extensive inclusion of perspectives and Traditional Knowledge of Indigenous Peoples. The assessment helped push global awareness of Arctic climate change into mainstream policy discussion.

L330: ### Arctic Marine Strategic Plan (AMSP)
L331: The first AMSP was endorsed by Arctic Council Ministers in November 2004 and set the Council's vision for the Arctic marine environment: "A healthy and productive Arctic Ocean and coasts that support environmental, economic and sociocultural values for current and future generations." An updated Arctic Marine Strategic Plan was published in 2015 to provide a framework to guide the Council’s actions to protect Arctic marine and coastal ecosystems and to promote sustainable development.

L410: ### Melting Ice: Regional Dramas, Global Wake-Up Call
L411: 
L412: Nobel Peace Prize laureate Al Gore, foreign ministers and climate change scientists met on 28 April 2009 in Tromsø, Norway to discuss the impacts of melting ice in the polar and mountain areas worldwide. The conference took place the day before the Arctic Council’s annual Ministerial meeting. A number of foreign ministers from states affected by melting ice and snow attended.

L420: ### Arctic Marine Shipping Assessment (AMSA) Released
L421: 
L422: The Protection of the Arctic Marine Environment Working Group (PAME) developed recommendations to guide the Council's work on Arctic shipping. This assessment evaluated the future of Arctic shipping as sea ice declines and influenced global maritime safety discussions and regulations providing the first comprehensive, circumpolar assessment of Arctic marine transport trends, risks, and policy needs.

L484: ### Establishment of the permanent Arctic Council Secretariat
L485: The decision to create a permanent secretariat was taken at the Nuuk Ministerial Meeting in May 2011. During the Swedish Chairmanship, the institutional capacity of the Council was strengthened and moved this decision into practice. The Secretariat was set up in Tromsø, Norway, and became operational in 2013, providing administrative support, continuity, and institutional memory. The formal endorsement of the Secretariat occurred in the Kiruna Declaration in 2013.

L524: ### Minimata Convention on Mercurcy was adopted
L525: 
L526: AMAP’s 2004 assessment results significantly contributed to the decision by UNEP to establish its ‘mercury process that ultimately resulted in the global Minamata Convention on Mercury that entered into force in 2017. This global treaty aims to protect human health and the environment from anthropogenic emissions and releases of mercury. To this day, the Minamata Convention has been signed by 128 countries.
